newsitem.title: FRANCE: Analyst predicts 202 million tonnes EU grain crop.
newsitem.headline: Analyst predicts 202 million tonnes EU grain crop.

text.p: Private analyst Strategie Grains on Friday forecast a slightly lower European Union grain crop this year at 202 million tonnes compared with last year's bumper harvest of 204.1 million tonnes.
The figure includes slight downward revisions for both years but leaves the percentage loss unchanged at around one percent.
In a previous report published in April, the French firm projected a total 1997 harvest of 202.6 million tonnes in the 15-nation EU compared with 204.2 million for last year.
Lingering drought fears point to a drop in average yields of three percent, which more than offsets a rise of two percent in the area sown to grain, it said in a new May survey.
But those fears have eased following recent rain, it said.
Despite this Spain, Portugal and the southern tip of France are still seen at risk from lower yields.
"It has rained everywhere in Europe since April 25 and drought worries have diminished," Strategie Grains said.
"Only the Iberian peninsular and the south of France have seen significant falls in yields until now," it added.
The 1997 harvest, supported by a drop in EU set-aside sowing limits, will however be well above the average for the previous five years of 182 million tonnes, its figures showed.
Pasta-making durum wheat, mainly grown in the drier south, would see the sharpest percentage fall in output, by five percent to 7.9 million tonnes, Strategie Grains said.
Barley would also show a wide contrast between area and yields, with output falling two percent to 51.7 million tonnes despite a four percent area increase.
Soft wheat, which makes up nearly half of EU grain output, would slip one percent to 90.4 million tonnes despite a two percent a sowings increase of two percent.
Maize output would be steady at 34.2 million tonnes, while rye production would rise two percent to 5.9 million tonnes.
Strategie Grains said weather conditions were "excellent" for grain in the northern European crop areas -- Scandinavia, Germany and the north of Britain.
The catch of rain since late April had helped crops in the big grain belt of central France as well as southern Britain. But average rainfall was needed from now on to moisten the soil.
Southern Spain and parts of southern France were looking at "serious" damage this year, it said, without going further.
France's cereals office on Wednesday predicted 20-30 percent yield loss in southern France, but said this would not have a major impact as only a small part of the crop was grown there.
Nearly four months without proper rain between January and the end of April had sparked earlier warnings of a drought year. --Paris newsroom +331 4221 5146
